title: Selective Exclusion
summary: Selective exclusion is the deliberate choice to leave parts of a system untouched while damaging the rest. In a ransomware context the actor avoids file types such as libraries, executables and shortcuts, and steers clear of directories and components whose corruption would immediately destabilise the host. The motive is operational and defensive at once. Encrypting an executable or a system library usually breaks running processes, so the machine reboots or applications crash, which is both loud and obstructive. Keeping core services alive lets the victim still see the ransom notice, communicate with the actor and pay. Avoiding certain folders also keeps security tooling and backup agents at least partly functional, or at least avoids the immediate behavioural alarms that mass modification of protected paths would raise. For defenders the value of this technique is as a detection hypothesis: a sudden, widespread pattern of file modification that conspicuously skips binaries, system directories and program files is far more telling than volume alone. Endpoint telemetry showing creation of files with a consistent new extension across user data, while executable paths and system folders remain untouched, is a strong signal. Backup and file integrity monitoring help here, because the excluded set itself becomes the fingerprint of the campaign.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker chooses to leave some files and folders alone on purpose. Ransomware usually scrambles as much data as it can. In this case it skips certain file types and system areas. It does that so the computer still works well enough to show a payment demand and keep running.
beginner.whyItMatters: If ransomware broke every program on the machine, the victim might never see the payment message. Attackers also avoid the folders that security tools watch most closely, so they can encrypt more before anyone reacts. For defenders, this strange pattern is useful. Data files change everywhere while programs and system folders stay untouched, which points to an attack. Watching for that shape is more reliable than watching for speed alone.
howItWorks: The attacker first studies the machine to learn where user data lives and where system files live.
Before encrypting, the ransomware builds a list of paths and file types to skip.
Common skips include program files, libraries and shortcuts, because changing them breaks running software.
System folders and folders used by security tools are often excluded as well.
The ransomware then encrypts the remaining files, usually adding a new extension, and leaves a text file with instructions.
Because key services still run, the machine stays responsive and the payment demand stays visible.
beginner.example: Picture a vandal in a hotel who wants the manager to find his note. He could smash every window, but then the building would be shut and nobody would read anything. Instead he ruins the furniture in the guest rooms. He carefully leaves the reception desk, the lights and the fire alarm working. The manager walks in, sees the note on an intact desk, and the place is still open for business.
takeaways: Ransomware often skips files whose loss would break the machine.
The pattern of what stays untouched can identify the attack family.
Monitor for mass file changes that conspicuously avoid system folders.

objectives: Define selective exclusion and explain why an attacker would leave data untouched.
List the file types and system areas commonly excluded from encryption.
Explain how keeping core services alive supports the attacker's extortion goal.
Describe the file change pattern that reveals selective exclusion to a defender.
Explain how file integrity monitoring and backups help identify the excluded set.
